questions.question: How are display: none, visibility: hidden, and opacity: 0 different?
questions.title: Hiding elements with display, visibility, or opacity
questions.direct_answer: display: none removes an element's generated boxes from layout; visibility: hidden keeps its layout space but hides the box and descendants by default; opacity: 0 makes the rendered box transparent while it still occupies space and can still receive pointer or keyboard interaction unless separately controlled.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses a hiding method by layout, interaction, and accessibility behaviour.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating opacity: 0 as a complete way to hide an interactive control.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State what happens to layout and focus rather than saying only visible or invisible.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: display: none removes the element's boxes from layout.
visibility: hidden preserves layout space and prevents ordinary interaction.
opacity: 0 preserves layout and only changes transparency.
A transparent control may still be focusable or clickable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`display: none` means the element and its descendants generate no boxes, so surrounding content lays out as if it were absent. In ordinary HTML use, hidden content is also unavailable to interaction and accessibility APIs until it is shown again.

`visibility: hidden` keeps the element's space in layout but does not paint the box. It is useful when the design must preserve geometry, and descendants can have special visibility behaviour, so I still test the actual subtree rather than assuming it is identical to display none.

`opacity: 0` paints the entire element fully transparent. Its box remains, and it can still receive pointer events or keyboard focus. For example, an invisible opacity-zero button may sit over another control and capture clicks, which is both confusing and inaccessible.

The choice depends on the desired hidden state. A closed disclosure usually uses the HTML `hidden` attribute or display none so it is absent from layout and interaction. A fading element may animate opacity, but its final inactive state must also remove or disable interaction deliberately.

None of these alone explains application state to assistive technology. I pair the visual behaviour with the correct HTML and ARIA state, such as `aria-expanded` on the controlling button, and keep focus out of content that is meant to be unavailable.

sections.title: Hiding has three independent dimensions
sections.content: Ask whether the element should occupy layout space, be painted, and receive interaction or accessibility exposure. The three properties answer different parts of that question, which is why substituting one for another can create empty gaps or invisible controls.

sections.title: Animation complicates the final state
sections.content: Opacity interpolates smoothly, while display has historically been discrete. Modern transition features can coordinate entry and exit in supporting browsers, but a robust component still defines a clear inactive state. During an exit fade, prevent accidental activation at the correct point and move focus before making focused content unavailable. Do not hide focus inside a transparent subtree for the sake of animation.

sections.title: What each hiding method preserves
sections.content:
| Property | Layout space | Painted | Can remain interactive |
|---|---|---|---|
| display: none | No | No | No |
| visibility: hidden | Yes | No | Normally no |
| opacity: 0 | Yes | Transparent | Yes |

sections.title: Make a collapsed region unavailable

How should focus move when a disclosure closes?

questions.question: What is the difference between moving an element with transform and with top or left?
questions.title: transform translation versus top and left
questions.direct_answer: top and left change the positioned box's layout offset, while transform: translate() changes the element's rendered coordinate space after layout. Transforms often animate more smoothly, but they do not cause surrounding content to reflow into the visually shifted position.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner separates layout geometry from visual transformation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using translate to make a permanent layout change that neighbouring content should respect.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect animation cost, containing blocks, stacking contexts, and final layout intent.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: top and left act on positioned layout offsets.
translate changes the rendered position after layout.
A translated element keeps its original layout footprint.
Transforms commonly suit motion; layout properties suit real geometry changes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`top` and `left` apply to positioned elements and influence where their boxes are laid out relative to a containing block. Changing those offsets can require the browser to revisit layout and paint work, especially when the change affects a substantial rendered area.

`transform: translate()` operates on the element after its normal geometry has been calculated. The original box keeps its place in layout, while the rendered result appears elsewhere. A transform also creates a stacking context when its value is not none and can affect containing-block behaviour.

For example, an off-canvas menu that slides in over the page is a good transform case because the page should not reflow during every frame. A sidebar whose wider width must push the article into a narrower column is a layout change and should not be faked only with translation.

Transforms are often composited and therefore a strong starting point for smooth motion, but that is not a universal performance promise. Very large layers, filters, paint-heavy descendants, and memory pressure can still cause problems, so I measure real frames.

I choose based on geometry first: if siblings must react to the new position, use layout; if the element should move visually over a stable layout, use a transform. Animation performance reinforces that choice but does not replace correct document flow.

sections.title: Layout position and painted position can diverge
sections.content: Translation changes where the element is drawn, not where the layout algorithm reserved its space. That is ideal for overlays and temporary motion, but wrong when the rest of the page must behave as though the element truly moved.

sections.title: Transforms bring stacking consequences
sections.content: A non-none transform establishes a stacking context. Descendants are then layered inside that context, which can make a high z-index child remain under content in a higher sibling context. Transforms can also establish a containing block for positioned descendants. When motion unexpectedly changes overlay placement or layering, inspect these side effects rather than only the translate numbers.

sections.title: Choose by the required effect
sections.content:
| Requirement | top / left | transform: translate |
|---|---|---|
| Neighbours respond to geometry | Possible layout model | No; footprint stays |
| Frequent slide animation | Often more work | Usually preferred |
| Creates stacking context by itself | Not simply from offset | Yes when transform is not none |

sections.title: Slide an overlay over stable page layout

followup_questions: Why can a transform create a z-index surprise?
When should a responsive layout use width or grid tracks instead?
How would you measure the difference in browser DevTools?

questions.question: When should you use CSS animations instead of the Web Animations API?
questions.title: CSS animations versus the Web Animations API
questions.direct_answer: Use CSS transitions or animations for presentation driven cleanly by selectors and media queries. Use the Web Animations API when JavaScript must create, inspect, pause, reverse, seek, coordinate, or await animation objects as part of application behaviour.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses declarative CSS or imperative animation control for a concrete reason.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming JavaScript animation is always slower or CSS animation can never be controlled from JavaScript.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that both share the web animation model and choose by ownership and control.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: CSS is concise for selector-driven states and reusable keyframes.
The Web Animations API returns controllable Animation objects.
JavaScript control is useful for seeking, coordination, and completion promises.
Reduced-motion and stable end states are required with either approach.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
CSS transitions and animations are declarative. A class, pseudo-class, or media query selects the state, and CSS describes how presentational values change. This is concise for hover feedback, disclosures, loaders, and other effects whose lifecycle follows styling state.

The Web Animations API exposes animation objects to JavaScript. Code can call `play`, `pause`, `reverse`, or `cancel`, set `currentTime`, inspect progress, and wait on a `finished` promise. That is useful when animation timing is coordinated with application logic or direct user scrubbing.

For example, a card hover lift belongs comfortably in CSS. A tutorial timeline with previous, next, pause, and a draggable progress control needs imperative access, so `element.animate()` and its returned Animation object are a better fit.

The choice is not a simple performance contest. Both approaches use the browser's web animation machinery, and the animated properties still determine rendering cost. JavaScript work around the animation can block the main thread, while poorly chosen CSS properties can also produce expensive frames.

I keep application truth outside the animation, provide equivalent reduced-motion behaviour, and choose the smallest ownership model that fits. CSS owns styling state; the API earns its complexity when code genuinely needs timeline control or completion coordination.

sections.title: Declarative state or imperative timeline
sections.content: CSS answers how a matched state should look and transition. The Web Animations API gives program code a timeline object. Both can animate the same kinds of properties, so control requirements are a better decision signal than a claim that one is universally faster.

sections.title: Completion should not be confused with business state
sections.content: An Animation's `finished` promise is useful for sequencing cleanup after an exit effect, but the application should update its logical state deliberately. Cancellation can reject or replace completion, users can request reduced motion, and a tab may throttle rendering. Treat the animation as one presentation path to a final state rather than the only mechanism that makes the state true.

sections.title: Pick the owner of the timeline
sections.content:
| Need | CSS animation | Web Animations API |
|---|---|---|
| Selector-driven hover/state | Excellent | Usually unnecessary |
| Pause, seek, reverse from controls | Awkward | Direct API |
| Await completion in code | Events available | finished promise |
| Respond to media queries | Natural | Requires coordination |

sections.title: Control one timeline from application code

followup_questions: What happens to the finished promise when an animation is cancelled?

questions.question: When should UI state use a class, an attribute selector, or a pseudo-class?
questions.title: Classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes for UI state
questions.direct_answer: Use native pseudo-classes for browser-known states such as :disabled, :checked, and :focus-visible; use semantic attributes when the DOM already exposes state such as aria-expanded or data-state; use classes for application-owned styling states that have no suitable native representation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner models state in HTML before choosing a convenient CSS hook.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding an is-disabled class without disabling the control or styling ARIA without updating its value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use one source of truth that supplies both behaviour and styling.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Native pseudo-classes reflect states the browser already knows.
ARIA attributes expose accessibility state and can also be styling hooks.
data-* attributes can represent application state without accessibility meaning.
Classes remain useful for purely visual or composite component states.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I choose a CSS state hook from the source of truth for that state. A genuinely disabled button uses the `disabled` attribute and can be styled with `:disabled`; a checked checkbox uses `:checked`. The browser then supplies behaviour, form semantics, and styling state together.

For disclosures, the controlling button needs `aria-expanded` so assistive technology knows whether its panel is open. CSS can select `[aria-expanded='true']` for the icon, which avoids maintaining a second `is-open` class that might drift out of sync.

A `data-state` attribute is useful for application states without a native or ARIA meaning, such as `data-state='loading'` on a decorative shell. A class remains simple for reusable visual variants such as `.card--featured` or when several internal conditions intentionally map to one style.

For example, adding only `.is-disabled` to a button changes its appearance but leaves it focusable and clickable. Setting `disabled` changes the actual control state and gives CSS the reliable `:disabled` hook. Visual state should not pretend to be behaviour.

I avoid duplicating the same fact across a class, data attribute, and ARIA attribute. One authoritative DOM state drives behaviour, semantics, and presentation where possible, which reduces bugs and makes inspection straightforward.

sections.title: Style the state where it already lives
sections.content: CSS hooks are not interchangeable if the underlying DOM behaviour differs. Native state should use native HTML, accessibility state should be accurate ARIA, and application-only state can use data attributes or classes. The selector follows that model.

sections.title: ARIA changes exposure, not built-in behaviour
sections.content: `aria-disabled='true'` announces a disabled state but does not automatically prevent clicks, remove the control from form submission, or apply `:disabled`. It is appropriate only when the interaction design intentionally needs an ARIA-disabled but still focusable element and JavaScript enforces the behaviour. A native button with `disabled` is the simpler, stronger choice in ordinary cases.

sections.title: Match state to its source
sections.content:
| State | Preferred source | CSS hook |
|---|---|---|
| Native disabled control | disabled | :disabled |
| Disclosure open | aria-expanded | [aria-expanded='true'] |
| App-only phase | data-state | [data-state='loading'] |
| Visual variant | class | .card--featured |

sections.title: Use one disclosure state for semantics and styling
